Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- A 13-year-old Minnesota boy who has cancer has resumed chemotherapy treatments and is not responding well, a family spokesman said Friday. Doctors say Daniel Hauser's lymphoma responded well to a first round of chemotherapy in February. Danny Hauser started a second round of chemotherapy treatment this week, Jim Navarro said in a statement on the family's Web site, dannyhauser.com. "The doctor changed the number of chemotherapy drugs in the protocol submitted to the court. Danny is not tolerating the drugs well and has been vomiting all day. He is understandably angry and depressed about being forced to go through the ravages of chemotherapy again." Daniel underwent his first round of chemotherapy in February, a month after he was diagnosed with Hodgkin's lymphoma. But his parents were concerned about the treatment's side effects, which typically include nausea, and decided to end the chemotherapy regimen and pursue holistic treatments instead. When Daniel's oncologist learned of the decision to reject standard treatment, which doctors say is associated with a cure rate of as high as 90 percent, he asked a court to intervene to ensure the teen got chemotherapy. Doctors say that, without it, the disease would likely prove fatal. But last week, before the court could act, Colleen Hauser packed up her son and flew with him to Southern California, from where they were planning to continue to Mexico to seek alternative alternative medical treatment. She said he would have run on his own had she not helped him flee. She changed her mind before crossing the border and returned this week with Daniel to Minnesota, where the family agreed to comply with whatever treatment the court ordered. A medical examination revealed that the boy's tumor had grown since he was diagnosed and the boy's doctor recommended he resume chemotherapy. After examining the boy on Monday, Dr. Michael Richards estimated the tumor's size at 5.3 inches by 5.1 inches by 6.3 inches, and said it was "protruding outside the chest wall." He said initiation this week of standard chemotherapy treatment was "imperative." Richards recommended at least another five cycles of chemotherapy followed by radiation, and added that the "goal will be to include alternative therapies in which the family is interested, as long as there is not data to suggest that a particular danger exists with any alternative medicine." District Court Judge John Rodenberg originally took custody of the boy away from his parents, but returned him to his family on the condition that they comply with the recommendations of the cancer specialist. Hodgkin's lymphoma is a cancer that affects the lymphatic system, which is part of the immune system. As the disease progresses, it compromises a body's ability to fight infection. CNN's Aaron Cooper contributed to this story.

Daniel Hauser, a 13-year-old boy from Minnesota diagnosed with Hodgkin's lymphoma, has resumed chemotherapy treatment following a contentious legal battle that captured national attention and raised profound questions about parental authority, religious freedom, and the state's responsibility to protect children's welfare.

## Background of the Case

Daniel was diagnosed with Hodgkin's lymphoma, a cancer of the lymphatic system that, when treated with conventional medical therapy, carries a remarkably high cure rate of approximately 90 percent. Despite these favorable odds, Daniel's parents, Colleen and Anthony Hauser, made the decision to halt his chemotherapy treatment after just one round, citing their family's adherence to a holistic healing philosophy rooted in Native American spiritual beliefs. They expressed strong objections to the harsh side effects of chemotherapy, preferring instead to pursue alternative and natural remedies they believed would be less invasive and more aligned with their values.

This decision quickly escalated into a legal confrontation when medical professionals and child welfare authorities intervened, arguing that stopping treatment posed a serious and potentially fatal risk to Daniel's life. A Minnesota court ultimately ruled that Daniel must continue his prescribed chemotherapy regimen, determining that the state's interest in protecting the child's life superseded the parents' religious and personal objections to conventional medical treatment.

## The Family's Flight and Return

In a dramatic turn of events, rather than immediately complying with the court's order, Daniel and his mother left their home and disappeared, sparking a nationwide search and prompting authorities to issue arrest warrants. The family's whereabouts remained unknown for several days, fueling media speculation and public concern over Daniel's health and safety. Eventually, facing mounting legal pressure and the risk of losing custody entirely, the family returned to Minnesota and agreed to comply with the court's mandate, allowing Daniel to resume his cancer treatment under medical supervision.

## The Challenges of Renewed Treatment

Since returning to chemotherapy, Daniel's experience has been far from easy. Reports indicate that he has suffered from severe and persistent vomiting, a common but distressing side effect of the aggressive drug regimen used to combat his cancer. Beyond the physical toll, Daniel has also shown signs of significant emotional distress, struggling to cope with both the invasive nature of the treatment and the psychological weight of having been thrust into the center of a very public legal and ethical battle.

Medical staff and family members have noted that the transition back into treatment has been particularly challenging, as Daniel now faces not only the physical demands of chemotherapy but also the emotional aftermath of the family's failed attempt to avoid it altogether. The difficulty of his recovery has renewed public sympathy for the family while simultaneously reinforcing the arguments of medical professionals who maintain that timely, consistent treatment is essential for achieving the best possible outcome.

## Broader Implications

Daniel Hauser's case has become a touchstone in ongoing debates about the boundaries between parental rights and state intervention when it comes to children's medical care. It raises difficult questions about how society should balance respect for religious and cultural beliefs with the imperative to protect a minor's life when a highly treatable illness is involved. The case has drawn attention from bioethicists, legal scholars, and medical professionals alike, many of whom point to the statistically high success rate of standard treatment for Hodgkin's lymphoma as a compelling argument for judicial intervention in similar situations.

As Daniel continues his treatment, his case remains a poignant illustration of the complex interplay between individual liberty, family autonomy, and the state's duty to safeguard the well-being of children facing life-threatening medical conditions.
